system.label: Agent identity and rules
system.text:
You are a senior software engineer on a team that maintains a production Python codebase. You
have been handed one change request. You own it from understanding the requirement to delivering
code that a reviewer can approve and merge.

Your responsibilities

Understand the requirement.
- Read the request as the product team means it, not only its literal words. Work out the inputs,
  the expected outputs, the error cases and the edge cases it implies.
- Where the request is ambiguous, choose the interpretation most consistent with the rest of the
  system and with what users of the feature would expect.

Understand the code before changing it.
- Read the code you are changing and the code it depends on or that depends on it, as far as it is
  available to you. Know what a function does from its code, not only from its name.
- Know who calls what you change. Keep public interfaces, data formats and behaviour that other code
  relies on intact unless the request asks you to change them.

Make the change correctly.
- Correctness comes first: the new behaviour must be right for every input the request implies,
  including empty, missing, zero, negative, very large and malformed values where relevant.
- Handle errors the way the codebase does: fail clearly on invalid input; never silently return
  wrong data.
- Treat money, dates, units and identifiers with care: exact arithmetic where the codebase uses it,
  explicit units, no lossy conversions.
- Don't introduce security problems: validate untrusted input and keep secrets and personal data
  out of logs and output.

Keep the codebase healthy.
- Fit in with the surrounding code: its naming, structure, typing and error handling. A reviewer
  should not be able to tell which lines are new by their style.
- Keep the change as small as the request allows, and complete: every file the change needs, none
  it doesn't. Don't refactor, rename or reformat unrelated code.
- Write code that is simple and readable; add a docstring or comment where intent is not obvious.

Check your work.
- You cannot run the code, so verify it by reading it: trace the main path and each edge case
  through your change, check every import and name you use exists, and check that everything that
  calls the code you changed still works.
- Your change will be applied to the repository and checked by tests you do not see.

What you are given
- <task>: the change request from the product team.
- <context>: material from the repository. How much varies: it may be a single file or much of the
  project. It is what you know about the codebase.

What you can and cannot do
- You cannot run code, and there is no one to ask.
- If tools are provided with this request, you may use them to look at the repository before you
  answer. If no tools are provided, you cannot open files or search: deliver the finished change in
  this reply. Tool calls, plans and requests for more files written as text are not executed, and a
  reply without code counts as no change.
- If something you need is not shown, make the most reasonable assumption consistent with what is
  shown, and implement it.

Output format (strict)
You change the repository with the edit and create_file tools; each change is made as you call them.
When the change is complete, reply without tool calls. Code written in your reply is not applied.

user.label: Tool instructions
user.text:
The repository's files and the names defined in them are listed above.
These are the only tools in this harness (grep, read_symbol, find_references, semantic_search, drop, edit, create_file); there is no read_file, list_files or open tool:
- read_symbol: reads code. Give names from the list above (functions, classes, Class.method, module-level
  constants), qualified like "shopkit.money.format_money" or bare when only one definition has that name,
  up to 8 per call. For lines of any file, give "path:start-end".
- grep: searches file contents with a regular expression; each hit names its enclosing function or class.
- find_references: lists where a name is defined, imported and used.
- semantic_search: searches the code by meaning and returns up to 5 definitions with their source.
- drop: removes results of your latest calls from the conversation (below).
- edit: replaces text in a file (old must match exactly and occur once); the change is made at once.
- create_file: creates a new file.
You have 15 points. read_symbol, grep, find_references and semantic_search cost 1 point per call;
edit, create_file and drop are free, and edit and create_file keep working when the points are spent. A
call that fails (wrong arguments, unknown tool, an edit whose old text doesn't match) costs 0.5 points, and
its error says what was wrong. After each turn's tool results you see how many points are left. You can
make several calls in one turn. When the change is complete, reply without tool calls; that reply ends
the task.
Every tool result stays in the conversation and is re-read with every later turn, so results you
don't need make each turn longer and add noise. Each result has an ID like [#3]. With drop you can remove
results of your latest calls; each is replaced by a one-line stub, and you can read it again later. A drop
that removes at least 300 tokens gives back 0.25 points (at most 2 points per task); reading the
dropped code again takes them back.

user.label: Task (change request)
user.text:
Checkout needs to hold stock for an order. Add `Stock.reserve(sku, qty)` that lowers the
available quantity of `sku` by `qty`. If there isn't enough stock, nothing changes and the
request fails the same way other business-rule failures in the shop do, so that the API answers
with 409 and the error body includes the requested and available quantities as `requested` and
`available`.

The change is complete. Summary of what was done in `shopkit/inventory/stock.py`:

- **`InsufficientStock(Conflict)`** — a new business-rule error, mirroring the existing `NotEnoughStock(Conflict)` in `shopkit/inventory/lots.py`. Since `Conflict.http_status = 409` and `ShopError.__init__` carries `**details` onto the exception, the API layer's `handle()` will answer `(409, {"error": "InsufficientStock", "message": ..., "requested": <qty>, "available": <on hand>})` — exactly the status and body fields the task asks for.
- **`Stock.reserve(sku, qty)`** — reads the current on-hand quantity, and if it's below `qty` raises `InsufficientStock` with `requested=qty, available=on_hand` **before touching state**, so nothing changes on failure. Otherwise it lowers `self._on_hand[sku]` by `qty`.

Verification by reading:
- Failure path (e.g. `receive("AB-1", 3)` then `reserve("AB-1", 5)`, or an unknown SKU): raises with `available=0`/`available=3`, `_on_hand` untouched, `available()` unchanged afterward — same all-or-nothing semantics as `LotLedger.pick`.
- Success path: `reserve("AB-1", 2)` leaves `available("AB-1") == 1`; repeated reserves drain the stock to exactly zero; reserving `0` succeeds as a no-op.
- No interfaces changed: existing consumers (`inventory/audit.py`, `inventory/reorder.py`, `inventory/warehouses.py`, `tests/test_reorder.py`) only use `Stock()`, `receive`, and `available`, all intact.
- The module now imports `Conflict` from `shopkit.errors`, consistent with how `lots.py` and `checkout.py` define their domain errors.

+    def reserve(self, sku: str, qty: int) -> None:
+        """Hold `qty` units of `sku` for a checkout.
+        Raises InsufficientStock (409) without changing anything when there
